facts.fact_text: On 21 September 2015 the applicant, together with Ms S., notified the Syktyvkar Town Administration of their intention to hold a 'picket' (пикетирование) on 25 September 2015 from 5 to 6 p.m.
The 'picket' notified on 21 September 2015 was intended to be held at the crossroads of Lenin and Kommunisticheskaya streets behind the Lenin monument in Syktyvkar.
The 'picket' notified on 21 September 2015 was expected to be attended by fifty people.
The stated aim of the 'picket' notified on 21 September 2015 was to 'discuss the arrest of the Komi Republic government'.

In his Internet blog post of 21 September 2015, the applicant stated that if the town administration proposed to hold the 'picket' on the outskirts of the town, a 'people's assembly' (народный сход), which did not require prior notification, would be held at the same location behind the Lenin monument.
In his Internet blog post of 22 September 2015, the applicant stated that a 'people's assembly' would be held instead at the same location and time as the originally planned 'picket'.
At about 7 p.m. on 25 September 2015 about fifty people gathered near the Lenin monument in Syktyvkar.
The 'people's assembly' on 25 September 2015 near the Lenin monument went peacefully and without any disturbance.
On 21 September 2015 the Syktyvkar Town Administration refused to approve the venue chosen by the applicant for the 'picket'.
The Syktyvkar Town Administration proposed that the 'picket' be held at one of the special locations for public events designated by the Komi Republic government.
On 24 September 2015 the applicant's VKontakte account was blocked by the VKontakte administrator.
The applicant's VKontakte account was blocked on 24 September 2015 following an order by the Federal Service for Supervision of Communications, Information Technology and Mass Media.
The applicant's VKontakte account was blocked on 24 September 2015 following an order by a deputy Prosecutor General of the Russian Federation.

The deputy Prosecutor General found that the applicant's VKontakte post of 23 September 2015 amounted to campaigning for participation in an unlawful public event in breach of section 10 paragraph 1 of the Public Events Act.

The applicant's VKontakte account was blocked pursuant to section 15.3(1) of Law no. 149-FZ of 27 July 2006 on Information, Information Technologies and Protection of Information (the Information Act).
On 25 September 2015 the applicant published a third entry on his Internet blog.

On 25 September 2015 the administrator of the Internet site that hosted the applicant's blog informed the applicant by email that access to the three blog entries (published on 21 September 2015, 22 September 2015, and 25 September 2015) had been restricted.
Access to the three blog entries was restricted on the order of the Prosecutor General's office.

The Prosecutor General's office ordered the restriction of access to the three blog entries because they had been found to contain calls to participate in public events held in breach of the established procedure.
The Syktyvkar Town Court noted in its judgment of 5 April 2016 that the Syktyvkar Town Administration had refused to approve the 'picket' at the location chosen by the applicant.

The Syktyvkar Town Administration's refusal of 21 September 2015 pointed out that Komi Republic regional law no. 91-RZ of 20 November 2012 [sic] prohibited the holding of public events in Stefanovskaya Square.

The Syktyvkar Town Court noted in its judgment of 18 November 2015 that the Syktyvkar Town Administration's decree no. 9/3483 of 4 September 2013 amended its decree no. 10/4160 of 28 October 2008 on locations where public events were prohibited.

The Syktyvkar Town Court noted in its judgment of 18 November 2015 that in accordance with the amended decree no. 10/4160 of 28 October 2008, it is prohibited to hold public events at the crossroads of Lenin and Kommunisticheskaya streets.

Section 5 of Komi Republic Law no. 91-RZ of 29 November 2012 on the Holding of Public Events in the Komi Republic prohibits the holding of public events in Stefanovskaya Square in the town of Syktyvkar.

Section 5 of Komi Republic Law no. 91-RZ of 29 November 2012 on the Holding of Public Events in the Komi Republic prohibits the holding of public events at railway stations, bus stations, markets, airports, educational institutions, buildings of educational institutions, religious buildings and areas within a radius of fifty metres of the entrance to those facilities.

Section 5 of Komi Republic Law no. 91-RZ of 29 November 2012 on the Holding of Public Events in the Komi Republic prohibits the holding of public events at children's playgrounds, locations designated by the municipal authorities for children's recreation and activities, pedestrian pavements, bus stops, and public parking areas.

Section 5 of Komi Republic Law no. 91-RZ of 29 November 2012 on the Holding of Public Events in the Komi Republic prohibits the holding of public events at buildings in a state of disrepair and areas within a radius of fifty metres of the entrance to such buildings.

Section 5 of Komi Republic Law no. 91-RZ of 29 November 2012 on the Holding of Public Events in the Komi Republic prohibits the holding of public events at buildings under construction, reconstruction or repair and areas within a radius of fifty metres of the entrance to such buildings.

Section 5 of Komi Republic Law no. 91-RZ of 29 November 2012 on the Holding of Public Events in the Komi Republic prohibits the holding of public events at buildings occupied by the regional authorities of the Komi Republic, Komi Republic branches of the federal authorities, the municipal authorities of the Komi Republic, state institutions in the Komi Republic and areas within a radius of fifty metres of the entrance to those buildings.

Section 5 of Komi Republic Law no. 91-RZ of 29 November 2012 on the Holding of Public Events in the Komi Republic provides that the listed prohibitions apply in addition to the locations where the holding of public events is prohibited pursuant to section 8 paragraph 2 of the Federal Public Events Act.

Syktyvkar Town Administration's decree no. 9/3483 of 4 September 2013 described the perimeter of the zone in the immediate vicinity of the Constitutional Court of the Komi Republic where the holding of public events was prohibited.

The perimeter described in Syktyvkar Town Administration's decree no. 9/3483 of 4 September 2013 comprised the entire Stefanovskaya Square and the adjacent streets, including the area at the crossroads of Lenin and Kommunisticheskaya streets.

In his appeal, the applicant submitted that the Syktyvkar Town Administration's decree no. 9/3483 of 4 September 2013, which allegedly prohibited public events at the crossroads of Lenin and Kommunisticheskaya streets, had never been published and was therefore not accessible to the public.

The Syktyvkar Town Administration proposed that the 'picket' be held at one of the special locations for public events designated by the Komi Republic government.

The deputy Prosecutor General found that the applicant's VKontakte post of 23 September 2015 amounted to campaigning for participation in an unlawful public event in breach of section 10 paragraph 1 of the Public Events Act.

The applicant's VKontakte account was blocked pursuant to section 15.3(1) of Law no. 149-FZ of 27 July 2006 on Information, Information Technologies and Protection of Information (the Information Act).

Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that inconvenience caused to citizens by a public event or an assumption by the authorities that there might be a risk of such inconvenience may not in themselves be considered valid reasons for changing the location or time of a public event (point 12).

Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that a necessity to temporarily divert pedestrians or traffic may not be considered a valid reason for changing the location or time of a public event, provided that it is possible to ensure that the traffic and the conduct of everyone involved in the event will comply with the established rules and will not lead to traffic accidents (point 12).

Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that disruption of pedestrians or traffic or a risk of disruption of essential public utility services may be considered valid reasons for proposing to change the location or time of a public event, provided that holding the public event will breach traffic or public transport safety requirements or limit citizens' access to residential premises or public facilities, irrespective of measures taken by the public authority to ensure compliance with such requirements (point 12).

Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that the public authority must submit to the court evidence of specific facts making it impossible to hold the public event at the chosen location or time (point 12).

Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that courts may not take into account any circumstances which were not mentioned in the proposal to change the location or time of the public event (point 12).

Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that courts should take into account that the public authority must suggest a specific alternative location and time for the public event compatible with its purposes and its social and political significance (point 13).

Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that if approval was denied because it was prohibited to hold public events at the chosen location, the public authority may suggest an alternative location for that event (point 13).

Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that the organiser must reply in writing, stating whether he or she accepts the proposed alternative location and/or time, no later than three days before the planned date of the event (point 13).
Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that the organiser may also propose another location or time for approval (point 13).
Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that if the organiser wants to change the date of the event, he must submit a new notification (point 13).

Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that public events held at private premises with unrestricted public access (such as shopping malls) must be notified to the public authority, and the organiser must enclose with the notification the consent to the public event signed by the premises' owner (points 8 and 14).

Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that it is not necessary to notify a public event planned at a specially designated location for public events, provided that the number of participants does not exceed the number permitted for each such location by regional law (point 15).

Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that the organiser must ensure the safety of participants and must therefore make enquiries about any other events planned at the same location at the same time to make sure that the maximum capacity of the location will not be exceeded (point 15).

Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that the fact that the organiser informed the public authority about the intended public event will be taken into account if he or she is held liable for failure to ensure public order and safety (point 15).

Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that the public authority may propose a change of location or time of a public event to be held at a specially designated location and not requiring notification only if another public event has been scheduled to take place at the same location and time and either the number of participants of the two simultaneous events will exceed the maximum capacity of the location, or it will not be possible to ensure the peaceful character of the simultaneous events by applying security arrangements habitually used at public events with a comparable number of participants (point 15).

Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that a cultural event, a fair or some other mass event not falling under the Public Events Act, scheduled to take place at the same specially designated location at the same time, may not in itself serve as lawful grounds for proposing to change the location or time of a public event (point 16).

Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that a cultural event, a fair or some other mass event not falling under the Public Events Act may serve as lawful grounds for proposing to change the location or time of a public event only if information about that mass event was duly published and it will not be possible to ensure safety at the two events if they are held simultaneously (point 16).

Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that if a court allowed the administrative complaint before the planned date of the public event, it may require the public authority not to impede the public event at the location and time chosen by the organisers (point 20).

Plenary Supreme Court Ruling no. 28 of 26 June 2018 provides that if the public authority has submitted evidence showing that new grounds objectively preventing holding the public event at the chosen location or time arose after the contested decision, the court may require that the public authority re-examine the issue of the event's location, time or the manner in which it is to be conducted within a certain time-limit (point 20).
